title: Improving your life, with the simple future

steps.title: One word where English needs two
steps.body:
English builds the future with a helper: *I **will** eat*. French does it with an **ending**, so the whole thing is one word: *je manger**ai***.

The endings never change, whatever the verb:

**-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont**

And here is the shortcut worth knowing: those are the present tense of **avoir** with the *av-* taken off — *ai, as, a, (av)ons, (av)ez, ont*. Learn them once and they serve for every verb in the language.

For regular *-er* and *-ir* verbs the stem is the **whole infinitive**. Nothing is removed. (A verb whose spelling changes in the present keeps that change in its future stem: *acheter* → *j'achèterai*, *essayer* → *j'essaierai*.)

*parler* → *je parler**ai*** · *finir* → *je finir**ai***

visuals.alt: A table of parler in the simple future, showing the whole infinitive as the stem with the endings -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont

check.prompt: Give the simple future *je* form of **regarder**.

steps.title: -re verbs drop one letter
steps.body:
Verbs ending in **-re** are the only regular group that changes, and the change is tiny: drop the final **-e**, then add the same endings.

*prendre* → *prendr-* → *je prendr**ai***

*attendre* → *attendr-* → *j'attendr**ai***

*boire* → *boir-* → *je boir**ai***

The reason is worth knowing: every future stem in French ends in **-r**. That is the sound of the future, and it is why the *-e* has to go. If your stem does not end in *-r*, it is wrong.

That one test catches most mistakes before they reach the page.

visuals.alt: A table showing how the future stem is formed for each verb group, with every stem ending in -r

check.prompt: Give the simple future *je* form of **vendre**.
check.solution: **Je vendrai.** Drop the *-e* from *vendre* to get *vendr-*, then add **-ai**.

steps.title: The irregular stems
steps.body:
A small group of very common verbs have their **own** future stem. The endings are still the same; only the stem has to be learnt.

These are worth knowing cold, because they are the verbs you will actually want:

- *être* → **ser-** : *je serai*
- *avoir* → **aur-** : *j'aurai*
- *aller* → **ir-** : *j'irai*
- *faire* → **fer-** : *je ferai*
- *pouvoir* → **pourr-** : *je pourrai*
- *devoir* → **devr-** : *je devrai*
- *venir* → **viendr-** : *je viendrai*
- *voir* → **verr-** : *je verrai*
- *vouloir* → **voudr-** : *je voudrai*
- *savoir* → **saur-** : *je saurai*

And one impersonal: *il faut* → **il faudra**, *it will be necessary*.

Notice that every one of them still ends in **-r**. The rule holds even here.

visuals.alt: A table of eight common irregular future stems, each shown as stem plus the identical ending -ai

check.prompt: Give the simple future *je* form of **aller**.
check.solution: **J'irai.** *Aller* has the stem **ir-**, which is the shortest in the language and the easiest to forget.

steps.title: Near future or simple future?
steps.body:
You already had one future from Year 9: **aller** + infinitive, the *near future*.

*Je vais manger* — *I am going to eat*.

Now you have a second. The difference is much the same as in English:

- **Near future**: close, already decided, conversational. *Ce soir, je vais me coucher tôt.*
- **Simple future**: further off, more formal, more of a prediction or an intention. *L'année prochaine, je mangerai mieux.*

Either is usually acceptable, and the examiner is not going to argue about which you chose. What earns credit is **using both** in the same piece of writing, because that shows range rather than one structure repeated.

A neat pairing: *Ce week-end je vais faire du sport, et à l'avenir je ferai de l'exercice tous les jours.*

steps.title: Turning a resolution into a sentence that scores
steps.body: A resolution on its own is one clause. Add a reason, a time phrase and a second tense and the same idea is worth several times as much.

visuals.fallback: améliorer — to improve; changer — to change; arrêter de fumer — to stop smoking; manger sainement — to eat healthily; faire de l'exercice — to exercise; boire de l'eau — to drink water; réduire le stress — to reduce stress; économiser — to save money; une habitude — a habit; en forme — fit.

steps.text: *Je ferai du sport.* — correct, one clause
*L'année prochaine, je ferai du sport.* — a time phrase
steps.note: Signals the tense to the examiner

steps.text: *L'année prochaine, je ferai du sport parce que je veux être en forme.* — a reason
steps.note: Reasons are the cheapest marks there are

steps.text: *Avant, je ne faisais rien, mais l'année prochaine je ferai du sport parce que je veux être en forme.* — a second tense
steps.note: Imperfect and future in one sentence

check.prompt: Translate into French: *I will improve my French.*
check.solution: **J'améliorerai mon français.** *Améliorer* is a regular *-er* verb, so the stem is the whole infinitive.

steps.title: Si takes the present
steps.body:
To talk about a condition, French uses **si** — *if*. And **si** never takes the future.

The pattern is fixed:

$$\textbf{si} + \text{present}, \quad \text{future}$$

*Si je mange mieux, je **serai** en forme.* — *If I eat better, I will be fit.*

*Si j'ai le temps, j'**irai** à la piscine.* — *If I have time, I will go to the pool.*

English does the same thing, which is why this half is easy: we say *if I eat*, not *if I will eat*. Keep it that way in French and you are right.

The halves can also swap round, and nothing changes: *J'irai à la piscine si j'ai le temps.*

if I have time, I'll go to the pool

steps.title: Your turn: the stems you need cold
steps.body:
The regular endings will look after themselves. What has to be automatic is the **irregular stems**, because they belong to the verbs you use most.

Cover the English and say each *je* form aloud. Then check it against the rule: does your stem end in **-r**? If not, it is wrong.

Use the speaker to hear them — several of them sound quite unlike the infinitive, and *j'irai* in particular is easy to miss in the listening paper.

visuals.fallback: je serai, j'aurai, j'irai, je ferai, je pourrai, je devrai, je viendrai, je verrai, je voudrai, il faudra.

check.prompt: Give the simple future *je* form of **pouvoir**.
check.solution: **Je pourrai** — *I will be able to*. The stem is **pourr-**, with a double *r*.

steps.title: Grade 9: quand takes the future, si takes the present
steps.body:
This is the point that separates the top grades in this topic, and it is the one place where French and English genuinely disagree.

English says: *When I **am** eighteen, I will travel.* A present, then a future.

French says: *Quand j'**aurai** dix-huit ans, je voyagerai.* **Future in both halves.**

The logic is that French is being consistent: both events are in the future, so both verbs are in the future. English is the odd one out.

The same applies to **dès que** (*as soon as*) and **lorsque** (*when*):

*Dès que j'**aurai** mon permis, j'achèterai une voiture.*

Now put it beside **si**, which behaves the opposite way:

| | French takes |
|---|---|
| **quand**, dès que, lorsque | the **future** |
| **si** | the **present** |

That contrast is the whole grade 9 point, and a sentence that gets both right in one breath — *Si j'ai le temps, je ferai du sport, et quand je serai plus âgé, je serai en forme* — is doing something a grade 7 answer does not.

The other habit worth having: use **three** tenses. Imperfect for what you used to do, perfect for what you have changed, future for what comes next. That structure answers most writing questions on this topic by itself.

*mais j'**ai arrêté** de boire du coca* — perfect, what has changed
*et à l'avenir je **mangerai** plus sainement* — simple future, what comes next
*Quand j'**aurai** plus de temps, je **ferai** du sport.*

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The simple future is **stem + ending**, one word: *je mangerai*.
- The endings never change: **-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont**. They are *avoir* in the present with the *av-* removed.
- For *-er* and *-ir* verbs the stem is the **whole infinitive**. For *-re* verbs, drop the final **-e**.
- **Every future stem ends in -r.** If yours does not, it is wrong.
- Irregular stems to know cold: *être* **ser-**, *avoir* **aur-**, *aller* **ir-**, *faire* **fer-**, *pouvoir* **pourr-**, *devoir* **devr-**, *venir* **viendr-**, *voir* **verr-**, *vouloir* **voudr-**, *savoir* **saur-**, and *il faut* → **il faudra**.
- **Near future** (*je vais manger*) is close and decided; **simple future** (*je mangerai*) is further off. Use **both** for range.
- **Si** takes the **present**, then the future: *si je mange mieux, je serai en forme*.
- **Quand**, **dès que** and **lorsque** take the **future**, where English uses a present: *quand j'aurai dix-huit ans, je voyagerai*.
- For a writing task, use **three tenses**: imperfect for the old habit, perfect for the change, future for the plan.

questions.solution: For *-er* and *-ir* verbs the stem **is the whole infinitive**: *parler* → *je parler**ai***. Nothing is removed.

questions.prompt: Give the *je* form of the simple future of **parler**.
questions.solution: **Je parlerai** — the infinitive *parler* plus the ending **-ai**.

questions.prompt: Which is the simple future ending for **nous**?
questions.solution: The endings are **-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont**. They are the present tense of *avoir* with the *av-* removed, which is why they are worth learning once.
options: -ons
-ez
-ont
-ai

questions.solution: **Je mangerai** — *I will eat*. The simple future is one word in French where English needs two.

questions.prompt: Give the simple future *je* form of **finir**.
questions.solution: **Je finirai.** *Finir* is an *-ir* verb, so the stem is the whole infinitive, plus **-ai**.

questions.prompt: Give the simple future *je* form of **prendre**.
questions.solution: **Je prendrai.** An *-re* verb drops the final **-e** before adding the ending: *prendre* → *prendr-* → *prendrai*.

questions.prompt: Which is the future stem of **être**?
options: ser-
êtr-
étai-
aur-

questions.prompt: Translate into French: **I will do more sport.**
questions.solution: **Je ferai plus de sport.** *Faire* has the irregular stem **fer-**, and **plus de** takes *de*, never *des*.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between *je vais manger* and *je mangerai*?
questions.solution: **Je vais manger** is *I am going to eat*, for something close or already planned. **Je mangerai** is *I will eat*, a little more distant or more formal. Using both shows range.
options: The first is the near future, the second the simple future
The first is past, the second is future
The first is future, the second is present
There is no difference at all in meaning or use

questions.solution: **L'année prochaine.** Also useful: *la semaine prochaine*, *demain*, *à l'avenir*, *un jour*.

questions.prompt: Translate into French: **When I am eighteen, I will travel.**
questions.solution: **Quand j'aurai dix-huit ans, je voyagerai.** The trap: after **quand**, French uses the **future**, where English uses a present. *Quand j'ai dix-huit ans* means *when I am eighteen* as a habit, which is not what is meant. Note also **avoir** for age, not *être*.
accepted: quand j'aurai dix-huit ans je voyagerai

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the tenses correctly after quand?
questions.solution: French puts the **future in both halves** after *quand*, because both belong to the future. English uses a present in the first half, which is exactly why this is examined.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the tenses correctly after si?
questions.solution: **Si** never takes the future. The pattern is **si** + present, then future in the other half: *si je mange mieux, je serai en forme*. Compare **quand**, which does take the future — the two behave oppositely.

markScheme.description: Si je mange mieux, je serai en forme

questions.prompt: Translate into French: **If I have time, I will go to the gym.**
questions.solution: **Si j'ai le temps, j'irai à la salle de sport.** After **si** the verb stays in the **present** (*j'ai*), and the other half goes into the future. *Aller* has the irregular stem **ir-**, so *j'irai*.

questions.prompt: Give the simple future *je* form of **venir**.
questions.solution: **Je viendrai.** *Venir* takes the irregular stem **viendr-**. It is worth learning with *tenir* → *tiendr-*, which behaves the same way.

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows the widest range?
questions.solution: The first uses imperfect, perfect and simple future, each with its own time marker. The others stay in one tense however long they run, and the third repeats *faire* three times.
options: L'année dernière je fumais, mais j'ai arrêté, et l'année prochaine je ferai du sport
L'année prochaine je ferai du sport et je mangerai mieux et je boirai de l'eau
Je ferai du sport, je ferai attention, et je ferai de l'exercice tous les jours
L'année prochaine je vais faire du sport et je vais manger mieux et je vais courir

questions.prompt: Écrivez environ 70 mots en français sur vos résolutions. Décrivez une mauvaise habitude que vous aviez, ce que vous avez déjà changé, et ce que vous ferez à l'avenir.
questions.solution: Three bullets, so three tenses: imperfect for the old habit, perfect for what has already changed, simple future for what comes next. That is the structure, and doing it deliberately is what the language marks reward.

Language: three tenses handled accurately, with a range of structures and connectives

criteria.text: A past habit described in the imperfect
A change already made, in the perfect
Future plans in the simple future, with at least one irregular stem

questions.modelAnswer: Avant, je mangeais beaucoup de fast-food et je me couchais très tard, donc j'étais toujours fatigué. Le mois dernier, j'ai décidé de changer: j'ai arrêté de boire du coca et j'ai commencé à faire du vélo. À l'avenir, je ferai du sport trois fois par semaine et je mangerai plus de fruits. Quand j'aurai plus de temps, je m'inscrirai à un club. Si je continue, je serai beaucoup plus en forme.

questions.prompt: Traduisez en français: *Next year I will eat more healthily. If I have time, I will do sport every day. When I am older, I will be fitter.*
questions.solution: **L'année prochaine, je mangerai plus sainement. Si j'ai le temps, je ferai du sport tous les jours. Quand je serai plus âgé, je serai plus en forme.** The whole translation is built round the contrast: **si** takes the present, **quand** takes the future.

examTechnique.body:
The simple future is mechanical once the stem rule is in place: every stem ends in **-r**, and the endings are *avoir* in the present with the *av-* removed. Check both before anything else and most errors disappear.

The marks that separate grades are not in the formation but in **quand** and **si**. French puts the future after *quand*, *dès que* and *lorsque* where English uses a present, and never puts it after *si*. Examiners test that contrast directly, in translation and in the writing task.

For writing, the reliable structure on this topic is three tenses: the imperfect for the habit you had, the perfect for what you have already changed, the simple future for the plan. It answers the question and shows range at the same time.

**Accents matter.** The app accepts an answer typed without them so a keyboard does not block you, but every solution shows the accented spelling, and the exam expects it.
examinerErrors: Building the future on a stem that does not end in **-r**, such as *je mangai*. Every future stem ends in -r without exception.
Keeping the final **-e** on an *-re* verb: *je prendreai*. Drop it: *je prendrai*.
Using the infinitive as the stem for an irregular verb: *je serai* not *je êtrai*, *j'irai* not *j'allerai*.
Putting a present after **quand** when the meaning is future: *quand j'ai dix-huit ans*. French needs *quand j'**aurai** dix-huit ans*.
Putting a future after **si**: *si j'aurai le temps*. **Si** takes the present, always.
Using *être* for age. It is **avoir**: *j'aurai dix-huit ans*.
Writing only in the near future because it feels safer. Using both futures is what shows range.
Listing resolutions without reasons. *Parce que* and *car* are the cheapest marks in the paper.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer gets the future after *quand* and the present after *si*, in the same paragraph, without apparently thinking about it. It uses irregular stems freely — *je serai*, *j'irai*, *je pourrai*, *il faudra* — rather than staying with regular *-er* verbs it feels safe with. It mixes the near future with the simple future for range, and it structures a writing task across three tenses: what used to happen, what has changed, what will happen. Every plan carries a reason.
